summary: Gives the detailed specifications for NetBIOS over TCP/UDP, including packet formats, protocols, and defined constants and variables. It supports local and internetwork operation and complements RFC 1001, which gives the general concepts and methods.

eli5.summary: If RFC 1001 is the plan for a house, this memo is the exact measurements: how each message is laid out and which values it uses.

questions: what is the netbios over tcp packet format
where are netbios name service details specified
what are netbios session packet types
subtitle: The exact packet layouts, codes, procedures and constants for NetBIOS over TCP and UDP.

tldr.problem: RFC 1001 explains how NetBIOS services can run over TCP and UDP, but implementers need exact packet layouts, field values, step-by-step procedures and constants to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1002 gives the formats of name service packets (modeled on DNS), session packets (a type, flags and length header over TCP) and datagram packets, then procedures for B, P and M nodes and the name server, and a table of defined constants.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard that pairs with RFC 1001. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 1002 is an Internet Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is read together with RFC 1001, which supplies the concepts behind these formats.

sections.title: Scope of the Detailed Specification
sections.content:
RFC 1002 contains the detailed packet formats and protocol specifications for NetBIOS-over-TCP. It is a companion to RFC 1001, which explains the concepts and methods. Bit and byte ordering are defined by the most recent version of the Assigned Numbers document that the RFC cites.

The RFC is organized in three parts: packet descriptions for the name, session and datagram services; protocol descriptions that give procedures in pseudo-code for each node type and for the name server; and a final list of defined constants and variables.
sections.eli5: This memo is the detailed rulebook. The earlier memo told the story; this one lists exactly what goes in every message.

sections.title: Name Format on the Wire
sections.content:
NetBIOS names in all packets (name, session and datagram services) use the "compressed" domain name message format defined in RFC 883. This is the "second-level encoding" described in RFC 1001. A name is a sequence of labels. Each label is a one-byte length followed by that many bytes, and the whole name ends with a zero length byte for the root.

For a NetBIOS name, the first label is the 32-byte first-level encoded name, so the first byte of the encoded name is 0x20. The RFC's example is the name FRED followed by 12 spaces in the scope NETBIOS.COM, which becomes EGFCEFEECACACACACACACACACACACACA.NETBIOS.COM at first level.

A label length is a 6-bit field, so a label is at most 63 bytes. The top two bits are flags: 11 means the next 14 bits are a pointer to a label elsewhere in the message, while 01 and 10 are reserved. NetBIOS implementations may use such pointers only in name service packets, never in session or datagram packets.
sections.eli5: Names are written like a web address, with each part starting with a number that says how long it is. Name-lookup messages may point back to a part already written to save space.

sections.title: Name Service Packets
sections.content:
Name service packets follow the structure of the DNS packet in RFC 883, with extra types and codes for NetBIOS. A packet has a header, question entries, answer records, authority records and additional records. Over TCP, each packet is preceded by a 16-bit unsigned length.

The header holds NAME_TRN_ID (a transaction ID the requestor makes unique per active transaction, and the responder copies back), an OPCODE with a response bit, NM_FLAGS, an RCODE result code, and four 16-bit counts. Opcodes are 0 query, 5 registration, 6 release, 7 WACK and 8 refresh. The flags are AA, TC, RD, RA and B. TC marks a message truncated because the datagram would exceed 576 bytes, in which case the requestor should use TCP to ask the name server.

Resource records of type NB (0x0020) carry an NB_FLAGS field and an NB_ADDRESS, the owner's IP address. The flags hold a group bit (G) and a two-bit owner node type: 00 B node, 01 P node, 10 M node.

The RFC then defines a packet for each operation: name registration, overwrite, refresh, release, query, node status, and the responses to them. Negative registration and release responses carry result codes such as FMT_ERR (0x1), SRV_ERR (0x2), RFS_ERR (0x5), ACT_ERR (0x6) and CFT_ERR (0x7). A NAME CONFLICT DEMAND is identical to a negative registration response with CFT_ERR. A WACK tells the requestor to wait longer, and its TTL field is the new time to wait in seconds. A redirect response, optional for the name server, sends the requestor to another NBNS.
sections.eli5: Every question and answer to the name helper has the same envelope: a ticket number to match answers to questions, a kind of message, a few yes/no switches, and then the name and address.

sections.title: Session Packets
sections.content:
All session messages travel over a TCP connection and share a four-byte header: a one-byte TYPE, a one-byte FLAGS and a 16-bit LENGTH. LENGTH counts the bytes after it, which is the size of the trailer. One bit of FLAGS (E) acts as an extra high-order bit of LENGTH, so the trailer can range from 0 to 128K bytes.

The types are 0x00 session message, 0x81 session request, 0x82 positive response, 0x83 negative response, 0x84 retarget response and 0x85 keep alive. A session request carries the called name and the calling name. A positive response always has a LENGTH of zero, and a retarget response always has a LENGTH of six, because it carries an IP address and a port. A negative response carries an error code: 0x80 not listening on called name, 0x81 not listening for calling name, 0x82 called name not present, 0x83 called name present but insufficient resources, and 0x8F unspecified error.
sections.eli5: Every phone-call message starts with a tiny label that says what kind of message it is and how long it is. Some messages are just the label.

sections.title: Datagram Packets
sections.content:
Datagram packets begin with a header of MSG_TYPE, FLAGS, DGM_ID, SOURCE_IP, SOURCE_PORT, DGM_LENGTH and PACKET_OFFSET. The message types are 0x10 direct unique, 0x11 direct group, 0x12 broadcast, 0x13 datagram error, 0x14 query request, 0x15 positive query response and 0x16 negative query response.

The flags hold a MORE bit and a FIRST bit for fragmentation, and a two-bit source end-node type: B, P, M, or 11 for an NBDD. A data-carrying datagram adds the source name, the destination name and the user data. A datagram error packet carries an error code: 0x82 destination name not present, 0x83 invalid source name format, or 0x84 invalid destination name format. Query requests carry just the destination name.
sections.eli5: A datagram has a header with who sent it, how big it is and whether it is one piece of a bigger message. Then come the names and the actual note.

sections.title: Protocol Procedures
sections.content:
Section 5 gives pseudo-code for each node type. A name service request always goes to the well-known UDP port, normally to the IP broadcast address or to the NBNS address configured at initialization. A response goes to the source address and port of the request. A demand must also go to the well-known port, to any target address.

A B node adds a name by broadcasting a registration request and pausing between retries. If no response arrives after the retry count, it broadcasts an update request and adds the name to its local table. A negative response means failure. P and M nodes follow their own procedures for adding, finding and deleting names, and for processing incoming packets and timers.

The NBNS procedures show the secure and non-secure behavior. For a unique name that already exists, a non-secure server sends an end-node challenge response and lets the end-node do the challenge; a secure server sends name queries to the old owner itself. If the owner is silent the entry is replaced and a positive response goes back, and if the owner replies the registration is refused. Members of a group name are not challenged, so a registration of a name that is already a group gets a negative response. The NBNS also discards any packet sent as a broadcast, and its entries expire at a multiple of the refresh TTL.

Session service procedures cover listen, call, data transfer and termination. A caller does name discovery, opens a TCP connection to the session port, and waits for a positive, negative or retarget response. If the response says the called name is not present, a P or M node tells the NBNS with a name release request.
sections.eli5: This part is the step-by-step recipe each kind of computer follows: shout or ask, wait a bit, try again a few times, then decide the name is yours or someone else already has it.

sections.title: Defined Constants and Variables
sections.content:
The last section lists the values that implementations share. The well-known ports are 137 for the name service (both UDP and TCP), 138 for the datagram service (UDP) and 139 for the session service (TCP).

Timing defaults: broadcast requests retry every 250 milliseconds, 3 times; unicast requests retry every 5 seconds, 3 times; the conflict timer is 1 second; the datagram fragment timeout is 2 seconds. The session service defaults are 4 connection attempts per call, a 30-second close timeout and a recommended 60-second keep-alive. The default maximum datagram length is 576 bytes, and a TTL of 0 is infinite. Several timers may be adaptive, and implementations may choose a longer conflict timer.
sections.eli5: These are the agreed numbers: which mailbox numbers to use for each service and how long to wait before trying again.

fields.name: NAME_TRN_ID
fields.desc: Transaction ID, copied from request to response.

fields.name: R + OPCODE
fields.desc: Response flag and packet type code.

fields.name: NM_FLAGS
fields.desc: AA, TC, RD, RA and B flags.

fields.name: TYPE
fields.desc: Packet type, such as 0x81 for a session request.

fields.name: FLAGS
fields.desc: Reserved bits, plus E as an extra high-order bit of LENGTH.

fields.name: LENGTH
fields.desc: Number of bytes that follow the LENGTH field.

items.label: SESSION REQUEST
items.desc: Caller asks for a session; carries called and calling names.

items.label: POSITIVE SESSION RESPONSE
items.desc: Accepts the session; LENGTH is zero.

items.label: NEGATIVE SESSION RESPONSE
items.desc: Rejects the session with an error code.

items.label: RETARGET SESSION RESPONSE
items.desc: Redirects the caller to another IP address and port.

items.label: DATAGRAM QUERY REQUEST
items.desc: Asks whether a datagram can be relayed.

items.label: DATAGRAM NEGATIVE QUERY RESPONSE
items.desc: The relay will not be done.
